units.t: Physics Basics. Episode three.
In this episode: How sound travels, Einstein's relativity, simply, Quantum mechanics, simply and Antimatter: the universe's missing twin.
Part one. How sound travels.
Every voice, song and thunderclap is just air being squeezed and stretched, and the physics explains everything from echoes to sonic booms.
A wave you can't see.
Clap your hands and you shove the air between them outwards.
Those molecules bump their neighbours, which bump theirs, and a ripple of squashed and stretched air spreads in every direction.
That ripple is sound.
It is a pressure wave, and the air itself barely moves: each molecule nudges back and forth and passes the push along, like a ripple running down a slinky.
When the wave reaches you, it pushes and pulls on your eardrum, which vibrates in step.
Tiny bones in your middle ear pass the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea, where thousands of hair cells turn it into nerve signals.
Your brain turns those signals into a friend's laugh or a favourite song.
The speed of sound.
In air at about 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels about 343 metres every second, roughly a kilometre in three seconds.
Light is nearly a million times faster, which is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
Count the seconds between flash and rumble, then divide by three to estimate the storm's distance in kilometres.
Sound is faster in warm air than cold, and much faster through liquids and solids, where closely packed particles pass the push along.
In seawater it travels at roughly 1,500 metres per second, and in steel several times faster again.
That is why you can hear an approaching train through the rails before you hear it through the air.
Pitch and loudness.
Pitch depends on frequency, the number of waves passing each second, measured in hertz.
The A above middle C, used to tune orchestras, is 440 hertz.
Young people typically hear about 20 to 20,000 hertz, shrinking with age.
Elephants use infrasound below our range, while dogs, bats and dolphins hear ultrasound above it.
Overtones make instruments sound different on the same note.
Loudness is measured in decibels on a logarithmic scale: every 10 decibels means ten times more sound energy, which we hear as roughly twice as loud.
A library is around 30 to 40, conversation around 60 and a loud concert well over 100.
Long or repeated exposure above roughly 85 decibels can permanently damage the hair cells in your inner ear.
Healthdirect can help with ringing or muffled hearing.
Echoes and the Doppler effect.
Shout across a valley and the sound bounces back as an echo.
Many bats send out rapid, high-pitched calls and judge the distance, size and texture of insects from the echoes, in total darkness.
This is echolocation.
Ships use sonar to map the seafloor, and medical ultrasound builds an image from echoes off organs, which is how many parents first see their baby.
An ambulance siren drops in pitch as it passes, though the siren has not changed.
As it approaches, waves bunch up and arrive more often; as it leaves, they stretch out.
This is the Doppler effect, described by Christian Doppler in 1842.
It works for all waves: police radar measures car speed, weather radar tracks wind in storms, and astronomers measure how fast galaxies move away.
Silence and sonic booms.
Films are full of roaring explosions in space, but real space is silent.
Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, and the near vacuum between planets has almost none to carry it.
Astronauts on a spacewalk talk by radio, which uses electromagnetic waves that need no medium.
Back on Earth, something interesting happens when an object travels faster than sound.
A supersonic jet outruns its own pressure waves, which pile up into a cone-shaped shock wave.
When it sweeps over you, you hear a sudden sonic boom.
The first officially confirmed supersonic flight was made by American pilot Chuck Yeager in the Bell X-1 rocket plane in 1947.
A cracking whip makes a tiny sonic boom too.
The key idea: Sound is a travelling ripple of pressure, not a stream of air rushing from the source to your ear.
Part two. Einstein's relativity, simply.
Moving clocks run slow, space bends, and your head ages faster than your feet.
Relativity is strange, and it's been confirmed again and again.
Light's fixed speed.
If you throw a ball forward at 20 kilometres an hour on a train doing 100 kilometres an hour, someone on the platform sees it move at 120 kilometres an hour.
Light doesn't work that way.
In 1887, Michelson and Morley tried to detect Earth's motion through a supposed 'ether' that carried light waves.
They found nothing: light's speed came out the same in every direction.
Light always travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, whether you move towards it or away.
In 1905, Albert Einstein, then a 26-year-old clerk at the Swiss patent office in Bern, took this as a basic law and followed it to astonishing conclusions.
Slow clocks, short rulers.
If light's speed is fixed for everyone, time must give.
A clock moving relative to you runs slower from your point of view: time dilation.
At everyday speeds the effect is tiny but measurable.
In 1971, atomic clocks flown around the world on airliners differed from ground clocks by billionths of a second, as predicted.
Muons, created when cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere, should mostly decay before reaching the ground, yet many arrive, because their clocks run slow.
Fast-moving objects also contract along their direction of motion, though travellers notice nothing.
Near light speed, each extra push takes more and more energy, and reaching it would take infinite energy.
The Large Hadron Collider pushes protons beyond 99.
999999 per cent of light speed, but never to it.
The twin puzzle.
Imagine one twin staying on Earth while the other flies to a distant star and back at close to light speed.
On return, the traveller is younger, perhaps by years.
It seems paradoxical, since each twin sees the other moving.
But the situations aren't symmetrical.
The traveller accelerates, turns around and comes back, changing reference frames.
The Earth twin doesn't.
The effect is real on small scales.
Astronauts on the International Space Station, moving at about 28,000 kilometres an hour, age a few thousandths of a second less than people on Earth over a six-month mission.
Spacetime and gravity.
In 1908, Einstein's former teacher Hermann Minkowski showed that relativity treats space and time as one four-dimensional fabric: spacetime.
Observers in motion slice it into 'space' and 'time' differently, so they can disagree about whether two distant events were simultaneous, and neither is wrong.
There is no universal 'now'.
General relativity, completed in 1915, covered gravity.
Einstein realised that free fall feels exactly like floating without gravity, which he called the happiest thought of his life.
Mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects follow the curves.
As John Wheeler put it, spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.
The theory explained a drift in Mercury's orbit and predicted that light bends around massive objects.
Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse expeditions confirmed it, making Einstein famous overnight.
Cosmic lenses, pocket proof.
A massive galaxy cluster can act as a giant lens, bending and magnifying the light of objects far behind it.
Einstein worked this out in 1936 but thought it would never be seen.
The first lensed quasar was found in 1979, and the James Webb telescope now uses lensing to study galaxies too faint to see otherwise.
A perfect alignment smears the background object into an Einstein ring.
Relativity also predicts that a spinning mass drags spacetime around with it, which NASA's Gravity Probe B measured around Earth, reporting in 2011.
Gravity slows time too: clocks run faster where gravity is weaker, so your head ages slightly faster than your feet.
GPS satellites gain a net 38 microseconds a day from both effects.
Uncorrected, positions would drift by about 10 kilometres daily.
The key idea: The speed of light is the same for every observer, however they are moving, and that single fact upends our ideas of time.
Part three. Quantum mechanics, simply.
The physics of the very small breaks every everyday rule.
Yet it's one of the most precisely tested theories in science, and it runs your phone.
Physics of the small.
Quantum mechanics describes how things behave at the scale of atoms and particles such as electrons and photons.
At that size, everyday ideas of cause and effect stop working the way you'd expect.
It sounds like science fiction, yet it's one of the most precisely tested theories in science, with predictions confirmed to many decimal places.
It's also practical.
Without it, we'd have no transistors, computer chips, lasers, LEDs, solar panels or MRI machines.
Your phone runs on it.
Energy in packets.
In 1900, Max Planck found that the colours of light from hot objects only made sense if energy is given off in tiny fixed amounts, which he called quanta.
In 1905, Albert Einstein showed that light itself comes in packets, now called photons, to explain how light knocks electrons out of metal.
That work, not relativity, won him his Nobel Prize.
In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed that electrons in an atom have only certain energy levels, like rungs on a ladder rather than a ramp.
Jumping between them gives off exactly the right amount of light.
That's why each element glows in its own set of colours, which astronomers use to work out what distant stars are made of.
A 'quantum leap' is actually incredibly tiny.
Waves and particles.
Light and matter behave like particles in some experiments and like waves in others.
In the famous double-slit experiment, electrons are fired one at a time at a barrier with two narrow slits.
Each electron lands as a single dot on the screen behind, like a particle.
Over time, though, the dots build up a striped interference pattern, which only waves make, as if each electron passed through both slits at once.
Try to detect which slit each electron goes through, and the pattern disappears.
Probability and uncertainty.
Quantum mechanics doesn't say exactly what a particle will do.
It gives probabilities.
Before it's measured, a particle can be in a 'superposition' of several possible states at once.
Measuring it produces one definite result, with odds the theory predicts precisely.
Schrödinger's cat, both alive and dead until the box is opened, was meant to show how strange this seems when scaled up.
In 1927, Werner Heisenberg showed you can't know a particle's exact position and momentum at the same time.
This isn't a flaw in our instruments; it's built into nature.
It's also why atoms don't collapse: an electron squeezed into the nucleus would have enormous uncertainty in its momentum, so it spreads out in a cloud instead.
Spooky links, new machines.
Two particles can become entangled, so that measuring one tells you about the other, however far apart they are.
Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance' and doubted it, but experiments have confirmed it repeatedly, and that work won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Tunnelling lets particles pass through barriers they classically shouldn't cross.
It helps power the Sun's fusion and is used in some computer memory.
The first quantum revolution gave us transistors and lasers.
A second is under way.
Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in superpositions of 0 and 1, to tackle problems such as simulating molecules for new medicines.
They're still experimental and error-prone.
Australia is a notable player, with research groups in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.
The key idea: Quantum mechanics describes atoms and particles, is among the most precisely tested theories in science, and underpins modern electronics.
Part four. Antimatter: the universe's missing twin.
For every particle there is a mirror-image twin with the opposite charge.
When they meet, both vanish in a flash of pure energy.
So why is the universe made almost entirely of one kind?
Predicted, then found.
In 1928 Paul Dirac combined quantum mechanics with Einstein's special relativity in one equation for the electron.
It worked beautifully, but it had a strange feature.
Just as the square root of four can be plus or minus two, the equation also gave solutions that seemed to describe electrons with negative energy.
Dirac took them seriously.
In 1931 he proposed they pointed to a new particle with an electron's mass but a positive charge.
In 1932 Carl Anderson found it.
His cloud chamber, sitting in a strong magnet, recorded cosmic rays from space.
He photographed a track that curved like an electron's, but the wrong way.
A lead plate across the chamber showed which way the particle travelled.
He called it the positron, and shared the 1936 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Total conversion.
Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge.
Electrons have positrons, and protons have antiprotons.
When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate.
Their mass becomes energy, usually as gamma rays, following E = mc².
It is the most complete conversion of mass into energy known.
Nuclear fission and fusion turn less than one per cent of their fuel's mass into energy.
Annihilation converts all of it.
The process also runs backwards.
A sufficiently energetic gamma ray passing near an atomic nucleus can turn into an electron and a positron.
This is called pair production, and it creates matter out of energy.
Building anti-atoms.
Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain led the team that created the antiproton at Berkeley in 1955, and won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics.
In 1995 researchers at CERN, near Geneva, combined an antiproton with a positron to make antihydrogen, the simplest anti-atom.
They made only a handful, and the atoms annihilated almost instantly.
Holding antimatter is the hard part, because touching the wall of any container destroys it.
In 2010 CERN's ALPHA experiment trapped antihydrogen in a carefully shaped magnetic field, and soon held some for around a quarter of an hour.
In 2023 ALPHA showed that antihydrogen falls under gravity, just like ordinary matter.
Useful, but not fuel.
Antimatter already works in hospitals.
A PET scan, positron emission tomography, uses a sugar tagged with a radioactive atom.
Busy tissue, such as some tumours, takes up more of it.
Each emitted positron meets an electron almost at once, and the two annihilate into gamma rays heading in opposite directions.
Detectors catch both and map the activity.
Positrons also occur naturally, in a very small fraction of potassium-40 decays, found in bananas and in you, and in some thunderstorms.
As fuel, antimatter disappoints.
It is made in accelerators one collision at a time, using far more energy than it could ever return, and it must be suspended in a vacuum.
CERN has noted that all the antimatter it has made would light one bulb for only minutes.
The missing antimatter.
Here is the deepest puzzle.
Our best theories say the Big Bang should have produced matter and antimatter in equal amounts.
They should have annihilated completely, leaving a universe of nothing but light.
Instead, there are galaxies, stars and people, all made of matter.
A small excess of matter survived, often estimated at about one extra particle for every billion pairs.
In 1967 Andrei Sakharov set out the conditions needed for such an imbalance.
Since 1964, experiments have found that some particles and their antiparticles behave slightly differently, but the differences found so far are far too small to explain it.
Why anything exists at all is still unsolved.
The key idea: Antimatter was predicted by an equation in 1931 and spotted in cosmic-ray tracks in 1932.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What actually travels from a sound source to your ear?
Answer. A ripple of pressure in the air.
Question two. What was so strange about the speed of light?
Answer. It is the same for every observer, however they are moving.
Question three. Why does quantum mechanics matter in everyday life?
Answer. It underpins technology like transistors and lasers.
Question four. Why did Dirac propose a new particle?
Answer. His equation's extra solutions implied a positively charged electron twin.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
